firstPrinciples.title: Periodontitis is bacterially triggered but host-determined
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Plaque is necessary, but how aggressively the disease destroys depends on the patient. Susceptibility is the bigger lever once plaque is present.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Bacteria start it, the host decides the damage

Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of bacterial aetiology that affects the supporting tissues around the teeth, but the host has an important role in susceptibility to the disease [1]. The pathogenesis is complex and the patient's response to the bacterial challenge is the major determinant of susceptibility, which is why identifying the various inherited and acquired factors influencing susceptibility is a core part of the periodontal assessment [2].

## Why this matters at the chair

Two patients with the same plaque score can have very different disease trajectories. Risk factor assessment (smoking, diabetes, stress, genetics) is not optional; it changes the prognosis and the treatment plan [3].

citations.quote: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of bacterial aetiology that affects the supporting tissues around the teeth. The host has an important role in susceptibility to the disease.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Introduction

citations.quote: The pathogenesis of periodontal disease is complex and evidence indicates that it is the patient's response to the bacterial challenge which is the major determinant of susceptibility. Identifying the various inherited and acquired factors influencing susceptibility is thus an important part of the periodontal assessment.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Risk factors

citations.quote: Susceptibility is thought to be partly genetically determined, which explains why periodontitis can affect members of the same family, although shared lifestyle, health behaviours and socio-economic risk factors are also likely to be common.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Chronic periodontitis

firstPrinciples.title: Smoking is the most important modifiable risk factor for periodontitis
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Tobacco use changes both the disease trajectory and the response to treatment, and it does so in a dose-dependent way starting from very low daily counts.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Dose-dependent damage

Smokers are up to **six times** more likely to show periodontal destruction than non-smokers, show a poorer response to treatment, and are at increased risk of recurrence [1]. The dose response is steep at the bottom of the curve: even smoking **1 to 4 cigarettes a day increases the risk of developing periodontitis by almost 50%** [2]. Long-term, smokers are roughly twice as likely to lose teeth [3].

## Why smokers respond worse

Reduced gingival blood flow, impaired white cell function, impaired wound healing and increased inflammatory cytokine production all push the host-bacterial balance the wrong way [4]. Clinically, smokers often have greater calculus, deeper pockets, more recession, more bone loss and furcation involvement, but **less BOP** because smoking masks bleeding [5]. That last point matters: BOP can no longer be used as an indicator of health in a smoker.

citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Tobacco and periodontal health

citations.quote: Therefore, patients should be advised that even smoking 1-4 cigarettes a day increases their risk of developing periodontitis by almost 50%.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Tobacco and periodontal health

citations.quote: Smokers are also twice as likely to lose teeth in the longer term.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Tobacco and periodontal health

citations.quote: This is thought to be due to a reduction in gingival blood flow, impaired white cell function, impaired wound healing and an increased production of inflammatory cytokines enhancing tissue breakdown.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Tobacco and periodontal health

citations.quote: Smokers often display: Greater calculus formation; Higher mean probing pocket depths and more sites with deep pockets; Greater gingival recession; Greater alveolar bone loss and furcation involvement; Less bleeding on probing.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Tobacco and periodontal health

firstPrinciples.title: Poorly controlled diabetes both raises periodontitis risk and impairs healing
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Diabetes is a two-way street with periodontitis: it raises risk, makes treatment harder, and unmasked diabetes can present first as periodontal disease.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Glycaemic control matters more than diagnosis alone

Poorly controlled diabetes increases the risk of periodontal diseases, and wound healing is adversely affected, especially when control is poor [1]. The reference assessment of control is **HbA1c**, with a target of **6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or lower** [2].

## A clinical signal that hints at undiagnosed diabetes

Patients with undiagnosed diabetes may present with **multiple, lateral periodontal abscesses**, in which case the BSP recommends liaising with the GP to confirm diabetic status [3]. The take-home is that periodontal abscesses in clusters are a screening trigger as much as a treatment problem.

citations.quote: Poorly controlled diabetes increases the risk of periodontal diseases. Wound healing is adversely affected by diabetes, especially if poorly controlled. This can make treatment of diabetic patients more difficult.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Risk factors: Diabetes

citations.quote: Diabetes control is best assessed using HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) values. People with diabetes are advised to maintain levels of HbA1c of 6.5% (48mmol/ mol) or lower.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Risk factors: Diabetes

citations.quote: Patients with undiagnosed diabetes may present with multiple, lateral periodontal abscesses in which case liaising with the patient's GP to confirm the diabetic status of the patient is advised.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Risk factors: Diabetes

workflows.title: Recording and acting on the BPE in adults
workflows.overview:
The Basic Periodontal Examination is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. It tells you the level of further examination needed and gives basic guidance on treatment. Used at every routine examination in patients with prior codes 0, 1 or 2; codes 3 or 4 trigger detailed charting.

## 1. Set up the examination

- Use a **WHO 621 (BPE) probe**: 0.5 mm ball end, black band 3.5 to 5.5 mm (and 8.5 to 11.5 mm)
- Probing force: **20 to 25 g**, equivalent to the force needed to **blanch a fingernail**
- Visually assess the gingivae first (redness, loss of stippling, location)

## 2. Divide the dentition into 6 sextants

- Upper right (17 to 14), upper anterior (13 to 23), upper left (24 to 27)
- Lower right (47 to 44), lower anterior (43 to 33), lower left (34 to 37)
- A sextant must contain **at least 2 teeth** to qualify
- All teeth examined except 3rd molars (unless 1st and 2nd molars missing)

## 3. Walk the probe and record the highest score per sextant

Walk the probe around the sulcus of every tooth in the sextant; record the **highest** score. If a code 4 is found, continue probing the rest of the sextant so furcations are not missed.

### Code definitions

- **Code 0**: pockets <3.5 mm; first black band fully visible; no calculus or overhangs; no BOP
- **Code 1**: pockets <3.5 mm; first black band fully visible; **bleeding on probing**; no calculus or overhangs
- **Code 2**: pockets <3.5 mm; first black band fully visible; **calculus or plaque retention factor** (e.g. overhang)
- **Code 3**: probing depth **3.5 to 5.5 mm**; first black band partially visible (pocket of 4 to 5 mm)
- **Code 4**: probing depth **>5.5 mm**; first black band entirely within the pocket (pocket of 6 mm or more)
- **\* (asterisk)**: **furcation involvement** detected; recorded alongside the number, e.g. 3\* or 4\*

## 4. Act on the score

### Code 0
- No periodontal treatment needed
- Repeat BPE at next routine check up

### Code 1
- Oral hygiene instruction (OHI)
- Plaque and bleeding charts
- Repeat BPE at next routine check up

### Code 2
- OHI plus removal of plaque retention factors (supra- and subgingival calculus, overhangs)
- Plaque and bleeding charts
- Repeat BPE at next routine check up

### Code 3
- OHI plus **root surface debridement (RSD)**
- Plaque and bleeding charts; **radiographs should be considered** to assess for attachment loss
- After initial therapy, record a **6-point pocket chart in that sextant only**

### Code 4
- OHI, RSD; assess need for more complex treatment; **referral to a specialist may be indicated**
- Plaque and bleeding charts; **radiographs should be taken**
- Record a **full periodontal chart** before and after treatment

### Asterisk (\*)
- Treat according to the BPE code (0 to 4)
- Assess need for more complex treatment; specialist referral may be indicated
- Plaque and bleeding charts; radiographs should be considered
- Full periodontal charting before and after treatment

## 5. Detailed periodontal charting (when codes 3, 4 or \* triggered it)

- Use a **Williams (10 mm)** or **UNC 15 mm** probe
- Record probing depth at **6 sites per tooth**; only sites **≥4 mm** need a number
- Always record **bleeding on probing** alongside
- Add recession, mobility, furcation involvement
- Probing depths **≥4 mm** are too deep to be controlled by tooth brushing and interdental cleaning alone

## 6. Caveat

BPE **cannot be used to monitor response to therapy**: it does not show how individual sites within a sextant change. Use the 6-point pocket chart pre- and post-treatment for that.

workflows.title: Periodontal screening for under-18s
workflows.overview:
Children and adolescents are screened with a **simplified BPE on six index teeth** to avoid the false-pocket problem of erupting permanent teeth. The codes available depend on the age band.

## 1. Identify the index teeth

Probe only six teeth:

- **UR6, UR1, UL6**
- **LL6, LL1, LR6**

Use the **WHO 621** probe; the second black band at 8.5 to 11.5 mm is useful where false pocketing is present.

## 2. Choose the code set by age

### 7 to 11 years (mixed dentition)
- Use **codes 0, 1, 2 only**
- This avoids the pseudopockets associated with erupting permanent teeth

### 12 to 17 years (permanent dentition)
- Use the **full set: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and \***

## 3. Code definitions for under-18s

- **0** Healthy
- **1** Bleeding after gentle probing
- **2** Calculus or plaque retention factor
- **3** Shallow pocket 4 to 5 mm
- **4** Deep pocket 6 mm or more
- **\*** Furcation

## 4. Refer when any of the following apply

1. **Aggressive periodontitis**
2. Incipient chronic periodontitis **not responding** to treatment
3. Systemic medical condition associated with periodontal destruction
4. Medical history that significantly affects periodontal treatment, or requiring multi-disciplinary care
5. Genetic conditions predisposing to periodontal destruction
6. Root morphology adversely affecting prognosis
7. Non-plaque-induced conditions requiring complex care
8. Cases requiring diagnosis or management of rare or complex pathology
9. **Drug-induced gingival overgrowth**
10. Cases requiring evaluation for periodontal surgery

workflows.title: Choosing radiographs for periodontal assessment
workflows.overview:
Radiographs are part of the periodontal record but only ever **retrospective evidence** of disease. Each exposure must be **clinically justified, of suitable quality, and benefit the patient**.

## 1. Decide if a radiograph is indicated

### Initial presentation
- Driven by clinical findings; routinely indicated for **BPE codes 3, 4 and \***
- Supports assessment of bone loss extent
- May follow detailed pocket charting if you want that information first

### Supportive periodontal therapy
- Used to track bone level changes over time, especially around furcations or where disease aggressiveness is uncertain
- Frequency by clinical need; **no clear evidence** supports a fixed interval

## 2. Pick the view

### Horizontal bitewing
- Useful early warning of bone loss, poorly contoured restorations and subgingival calculus
- Standard positioning gives a non-distorted view of bone in relation to the **CEJ**

### Vertical bitewing
- Better visualisation of bone level than horizontal bitewing
- Hard to position in shallow palates; may need periapicals for apical status

### Periapical (long-cone paralleling)
- **Gold standard for periodontal assessment**
- Non-distorted 2D picture of bone in relation to CEJ and total root length
- Use a beam-aiming device for consistency

### Dental panoramic tomograph (DPT)
- **Not for routine screening**: yield is low for the dose
- Consider in complex cases with multiple dental concerns

### Periapical vs panoramic
- Full mouth periapicals = more accurate detail of bony defects
- Good DPT = quicker, more comfortable, useful overview, but distorts in anterior sextants and may need periapical supplements
- Use **rectangular collimation** on periapicals and **field-size collimation** on DPTs to minimise dose

## 3. Report the radiograph in the notes

Medicolegally, document image quality and assess for:

- **Degree of bone loss**: if apex visible, report as **% of root length**
- **Pattern of bone loss**: horizontal vs angular (vertical)
- **Furcation defects**
- **Subgingival calculus**
- Other features: perio-endo lesions, widened PDL spaces, abnormal root length or morphology, overhanging restorations

## 4. Use radiographs to set treatment expectations

- Angular defects **>3 mm** deep: do **not** expect dramatic pocket reductions with simple non-surgical therapy
- Multiple angular defects **plus furcation involvement** suggest complex treatment need and consideration for **referral**

workflows.title: Building a full periodontal diagnosis
workflows.overview:
After the BPE, detailed charting and radiographs, the diagnosis is **constructed from three independent decisions**: type, extent (distribution), and severity.

## 1. Take the history and listen

Use open questions: what, when, where, why, how. Then specifics:

1. Do your gums bleed on brushing or overnight?
2. Are any of your teeth loose?
3. Can you chew everything you want to?
4. Do you have a bad taste or smell from your mouth?
5. Do you suffer from pain, swelling, gumboils or blisters?
6. Do you smoke?
7. Is there anything else you would like to tell me?

## 2. Run the special investigations indicated by the BPE code

- **0**: none
- **1, 2**: plaque and bleeding charts, risk factor assessment
- **3**: plaque and bleeding charts, risk factor assessment, **consider radiographs**; detailed charting of sextants scoring 3 after treatment
- **4**: full detailed periodontal charting before and after treatment, **radiographs should be taken**, plaque and bleeding charts, risk factor assessment
- **\***: treat according to BPE code (0 to 4); radiographs should be considered

## 3. Use the probe to answer two questions

1. **Where is the base of the gingival crevice?** Recession added to probing depth gives the **clinical attachment loss (CAL)**, the better long-term parameter, although the CEJ is often hard to find.
2. **Does the tissue bleed on probing?** Bleeding from the gingival margin = **gingivitis**; bleeding from the base of the pocket = **periodontitis**, and is the indicator that responds to root debridement. **Absence of BOP from the bottom of the pocket predicts periodontal stability**. Smokers may not bleed despite disease.

## 4. Construct the diagnosis (three steps)

### Step 1: type

- **No attachment loss, no inflammation** → health
- **No attachment loss, inflammation present** → gingivitis
- **Attachment loss, plaque level matches the loss, no other systemic condition** → **chronic periodontitis**
- **Attachment loss, plaque level inconsistent with the loss (often little plaque or calculus, vertical bone defects, family history, age <35, otherwise healthy)** → consider **aggressive periodontitis**

### Step 2: extent

- **>30%** of sites involved → **generalised**
- **<30%** of sites involved → **localised**

### Step 3: severity (by attachment loss)

- **Mild**: 1 to 2 mm
- **Moderate**: 3 to 4 mm
- **Severe**: ≥ 5 mm

## 5. Stitch the elements together

E.g. *Moderate generalised chronic periodontitis (smoking-associated)*. The diagnosis must come **before** prognosis and treatment plan.

firstPrinciples.title: Bleeding on probing only signals stability when it is absent from the pocket base
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: BOP is the most useful single sign in periodontology, but its meaning depends on where the bleeding is coming from and whether the patient smokes.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the bleed location tells you

Bleeding on probing is a measure of inflammation, not necessarily of active tissue destruction [1]. Bleeding from the **gingival margin** indicates gingivitis and responds quickly to improvements in plaque removal. Bleeding from the **base of the pocket** represents periodontitis and is more reflective of the response to root debridement [2].

## Absence of BOP predicts stability

The most useful clinical inference is the negative one: an absence of BOP from the bottom of the pocket predicts periodontal stability and is a useful indicator at the reassessment stage [3]. The big caveat is smoking: in smokers, bleeding is hidden, so absence of BOP cannot be relied upon as a sign of health [4].

firstPrinciples.title: Probing depth above 4 mm is the threshold for active intervention
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Once a pocket is too deep for a brush and floss to reach the bottom, host hygiene alone cannot maintain it. The 4 mm rule is what divides maintenance from active care.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What 4 mm means biologically

The probing depth at any site dictates the patient's ability to maintain soft tissue health by optimal plaque control. **Probing depths of 4 mm or more are considered to be too deep to be controlled by tooth brushing and interdental cleaning alone**, and these sites should be considered for active periodontal therapy [1].

## Why this drives the post-treatment workflow

This is also why the SPT appointment escalates instrumentation when pockets exceed 4 mm: more rigorous root surface debridement is needed for pockets deeper than 4 mm, especially those with bleeding on probing [2].

firstPrinciples.title: Aggressive periodontitis is recognised by the mismatch between plaque and destruction, not by severity alone
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Aggressive periodontitis is rare but specific. Its diagnosis is pattern-based, not threshold-based, and the pattern hinges on the disconnect between plaque load and attachment loss.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The clinical pattern

Approximately 1 in every 1000 patients suffers more rapid attachment loss [1]. Aggressive periodontitis is diagnosed from its rapid rate of progress or as a result of severe disease in individuals usually under 35 years of age who are otherwise medically healthy (with absence of other risk factors such as tobacco use), and with evidence of other close family members affected. It is often characterised by **vertical bone defects on radiographs**, and there may be **little plaque or calculus present** [2].

## How the diagnostic logic works

The key signal in the chair is the mismatch: if the level of plaque is consistent with the level of attachment loss the most likely diagnosis is chronic periodontitis, but if the level of plaque is inconsistent with the amount of attachment loss then aggressive periodontitis should be considered [3]. The implication is that a young, low-plaque patient with vertical defects and a family history is the textbook presentation, and the action is referral.

workflows.title: Delivering non-surgical periodontal therapy
workflows.overview:
Non-surgical therapy is the **first-line approach** for almost all patients with periodontitis. It is highly effective for early to moderate disease. The phases run in order: behaviour change, debridement, then reassessment.

## 1. Set the principles

Modern concepts:

- **Effective patient-performed oral hygiene is critical** to success
- Effects of OHI are short-term: regular advice and encouragement is needed for long-term change
- Plaque biofilms (attached and non-attached) in the sulcus and pockets must be regularly removed
- **Plaque retentive factors** (calculus, restoration overhangs) must be eliminated

What this achieves:

- Controls the bacterial challenge
- Addresses local risk factors
- Minimises systemic risk factors
- Resolves inflammation, alters putative pathogens, restores periodontal health

## 2. Behaviour change first

Use Oral Hygiene **TIPPS**:

1. **Talk** about the causes of periodontal disease and barriers to plaque removal
2. **Instruct** on effective plaque removal
3. Have the patient **Practise** in the surgery; check confidence (a key predictor of success)
4. Agree a **Plan** the patient owns, with their own goals
5. **Support** the patient at follow-up

Use open questions, deliver information in small doses, reflect, guide rather than direct, talk adult-to-adult, and **position the patient upright at or just above your eye level**.

## 3. Address risk factors

- Smoking: brief advice, refer to NHS Smokefree, document pack-years
- Diabetes: assess control with **HbA1c (target ≤6.5% / 48 mmol/mol)**; liaise with GP if needed
- Stress: recognise and modify treatment plan if needed
- Drug-induced gingival overgrowth: liaise with medical colleagues about alternatives

## 4. Root surface debridement

The key elements of good results:

- **Good scaling skills** (practise on extracted teeth)
- Well-maintained instruments: Universal and Gracey curettes (sharpened); ultrasonic and sonic tips for deep pockets and furcations; monitor tip wear
- **Time**: it can take several minutes per tooth in deep pockets. Furcations, root grooves and infrabony pockets make debridement harder. **One or two long appointments can be as effective as four spread out**, balancing operator and patient fatigue

Hand vs powered instruments: few differences in effectiveness in experienced hands.

## 5. Manage the side effects

Warn the patient at consent stage about:

- Increased gingival recession (longer-looking teeth)
- Black triangles
- Increased dentine sensitivity
- Soreness, food packing
- Risk of prolonged sensitivity from excessive root surface debridement

For hypersensitivity, offer toothpastes containing **potassium salts, oxalates or arginine**.

## 6. Use chemotherapeutics sparingly

- **0.2% chlorhexidine digluconate mouthrinse**: licensed for **30 days only**; useful when cleaning is difficult; not routine
- **Subgingival irrigation with chlorhexidine**: no clinical benefit shown
- Effective subgingival debridement is the mainstay; chemicals are an adjunct at most

## 7. Reassess

Decide between maintenance, further non-surgical therapy, or surgical referral. Reassessment timing is typically:

- **6 weeks** for oral hygiene response
- **12 weeks post-RSD** for repeat periodontal charting

Probing depth changes of **up to 2 mm** could simply be measurement error, so the **same clinician** should ideally repeat the charting.

workflows.title: Using antimicrobials in periodontitis
workflows.overview:
Antimicrobials have **very little place** in routine periodontal therapy. Antibiotic resistance, anaphylaxis risk and modest benefit mean the bar for prescribing is high. Wherever possible, drainage of infection and removal of cause replace antibiotics in systemically well patients.

## 1. Decide if a systemic antibiotic is even indicated

### Chronic periodontitis
- **No indication** for systemic antibiotics

### Aggressive periodontitis
- May be indicated, but evidence on benefit vs risk is unclear
- Suggested approach: initial non-surgical therapy without antibiotics, only consider antibiotics if results are poor despite excellent OH and effective RSD
- **Refer for specialist care** where available

### Necrotising periodontal diseases
- **Metronidazole 200 mg t.d.s for 3 days** (covers fuso-spirochaetal anaerobes)
- Plus: address smoking, stress, oral hygiene and diet

### Periodontal abscess
- **Single abscess**: drain via instrumentation or incision; **not antibiotics**
- **With systemic involvement** (fever, malaise, facial swelling): antibiotics **plus** debridement
- **Multiple lateral abscesses**: rule out **undiagnosed diabetes** and refer for tests

## 2. Prescribe correctly when treating aggressive periodontitis

- Give at the **end** of a thorough subgingival debridement compressed into **7 to 10 days**
- **Combination of choice**: amoxicillin + metronidazole, **starting on the day of the final debridement**
- Never use systemic antibiotics in isolation; always as an adjunct to professional mechanical therapy

### Doses

- **Amoxicillin 500 mg t.d.s for 7 days** (UK dose)
- **Metronidazole 200 mg t.d.s for 7 days**
- Penicillin allergy: **doxycycline 100 mg OD for 21 days**, with a **200 mg loading dose** on day 1
- A longer course is more likely to be met with non-compliance

## 3. Local delivery antibiotics

Indications are limited:

- **Only after non-surgical treatment** (not first-line)
- For **isolated pockets** that have failed to respond to repeated conventional treatment
- **No detectable calculus** at the site
- **Good plaque control** maintained

Benefit is **modest**. If isolated sites are not responding despite good plaque control, **consider referral**.

workflows.title: Running supportive periodontal therapy (SPT)
workflows.overview:
Supportive periodontal therapy is the **maintenance regime** that follows initial periodontal therapy. The goal is low inflammation and good oral hygiene, with appointment intervals tailored to risk and stability.

## 1. Set the recall interval by risk

### Patients without periodontitis (BPE 0 to 2)
- Hygienist visit **every 1 to 2 years** for many patients
- Around **50%** may still develop periodontitis if causative and risk factors are not controlled

### Patients diagnosed with periodontitis
- **Three-monthly recall** is the typical starting interval
- Justification: pathogenic flora can re-establish at the base of a 5 mm + pocket **three months** after thorough subgingival debridement, even with good home care
- Initially intervals **2 to 4 months**, reviewed at each visit
- Stable, compliant patients with stable supra- and subgingival environments may have intervals **extended over time**

## 2. Watch the high-risk sites

Certain sites stay difficult and need closer monitoring:

- **Furcations**
- Pockets associated with **infrabony defects**
- Pockets associated with root grooves, enamel projections, or chronic food impaction sites

## 3. Run the SPT appointment

1. Oral examination with recording of plaque and gingival inflammation (redness, bleeding), used for re-motivation in the affected areas
2. Check probing depths and bleeding from the pocket
3. Supra- and subgingival ultrasonic and hand scaling to remove plaque or calculus
4. **More rigorous RSD** for pockets **>4 mm**, especially with BOP
5. Local anaesthetic if needed for deep residual pockets (cross-reference last periodontal chart)
6. **Periodontal charting repeated annually**

## 4. Monitor the patient and the sites

In consultation with the hygienist, monitor over multiple appointments:

- Has the patient stopped smoking?
- General plaque levels across recent visits?
- Any **repeated BOP at a specific site**?
- Any **2 mm increase in probing depth** at a specific site?

Set expectations from the start: the patient must understand that once active treatment ends, **regular maintenance is for life**.

workflows.title: Deciding when to refer a periodontitis patient
workflows.overview:
BSP guidance grades cases by **complexity**, then maps complexity to who should treat. Initial non-surgical therapy must still be commenced in general practice as part of the GDP's duty of care, even when onward referral is planned.

## 1. Identify the complexity level

### Level 1 (general practice)
- Diagnosis and management of uncomplicated periodontal diseases
- Risk evaluation, BPE, OHI, RSD, supportive periodontal care
- Avoidance of antibiotic use except in necrotising periodontal disease or acute abscess with systemic complications
- Preventive and supportive care for implants

### Level 2 (general practice if skilled, otherwise refer)
- After primary care therapy: residual **moderate (30 to 50% horizontal bone loss)** chronic periodontitis with residual true pockets ≥6 mm
- Certain non-plaque-induced diseases (viral, autoimmune, vesiculo-bullous, GI manifestations) under specialist guidance
- **Aggressive periodontitis** as determined by a specialist at referral
- Furcation defects in **strategically important teeth**
- Non-surgical management of gingival enlargement, in collaboration with medical colleagues
- Pocket reduction surgery when delegated by a specialist
- Peri-implant **mucositis** where implants placed under NHS contract

### Level 3 (refer)
- **Severe (>50% horizontal bone loss)** periodontitis, aggressive periodontitis and true pocketing ≥6 mm
- Periodontal **surgery**
- Furcation defects and complex root morphologies not suitable for delegation
- Non-plaque-induced diseases not suitable for delegation
- **Peri-implantitis** under NHS contract
- Multi-disciplinary specialist care
- Level 2 cases that did not respond

## 2. Apply modifying factors (each adds one increment, not cumulative)

- Medical history that significantly affects clinical management
- Co-ordinated medical or dental multi-disciplinary care
- Special needs for acceptance or provision of dental treatment
- Concurrent mucogingival disease (e.g. erosive lichen planus)
- Head/neck radiotherapy or IV bisphosphonate therapy
- Significantly immuno-compromised or immunosuppressed
- Significant bleeding dyscrasia or disorder
- Potential drug interaction

## 3. Apply the routing rule

1. **Level 1** → treat in general practice
2. **Level 2** → treat in general practice **if you have the skills**, otherwise refer
3. **Level 3** → refer the majority
4. **Aggressive periodontitis** → offer referral after initial preventive advice and OHI
5. **Chronic periodontitis** → initial care in general practice; refer if unsuccessful
6. **Modifying factors** may move a patient to the next level

## 4. Carry out the GDP duty before referral

Even when onward referral is planned:

- Commence initial **non-surgical periodontal therapy** in general practice
- Address other primary dental pathology (caries, endodontic lesions)
- Control modifiable risk factors, particularly **smoking** (refer to cessation services if needed)

## 5. Refer correctly

The referral letter should include:

- Patient name, DOB, contact details
- Reason for referral, patient concerns, any emergency problems
- Relevant medical history including smoking history and all medications
- Details of any periodontal treatment already carried out
- Relevant radiographs (especially old ones) and charts

Keep a copy with the patient's notes; record the referral and reason in the chart.

## 6. If the patient declines

- Listen to the reason; address misunderstandings
- Ensure the patient understands the consequences
- **Document the discussion**
- Continue monitoring; offer best preventive advice; ask again at recall

workflows.title: Tobacco cessation in periodontal patients
workflows.overview:
Smoking is the **single most important modifiable risk factor** for periodontitis. The dentist has a duty to identify it, document it, and intervene.

## 1. Ask, document, and re-record

- Ask about tobacco use; document at every regular recall
- Record current self-reported smoking status
- Record the **historic burden** in **pack-years** (packs/day × years smoked)

## 2. Counsel the patient on the impact

- Smoking 1 to 4 cigarettes/day raises periodontitis risk by ~**50%**
- Smokers up to **6×** more likely to show periodontal destruction than non-smokers
- Smokers are **twice as likely** to lose teeth long-term
- Smokers show poorer treatment response (even with good OH) and higher recurrence risk
- Cigars, cannabis and smokeless tobacco carry **similar risk** to cigarettes
- E-cigarettes likely less harmful than cigarettes but **not as good as not smoking**; evidence gap
- A characteristic smoker presentation: **less BOP** (masking), greater calculus, deeper pockets, more recession, more bone loss and furcation involvement

## 3. Match the intervention to readiness

### Patient considering quitting
- Refer to specialist quit smoking services (e.g. **NHS Smokefree**)

### Patient unwilling to take up such a service
- You or a delegated team member should provide **brief tobacco cessation advice**

### Patient who has tried and failed before
- Reframe: stopping is a **process not an event**; on average it takes about **7 serious attempts**
- Each failed attempt is another milestone, not a defeat

## 4. Warn about the rebound

On smoking cessation, the patient may notice a **transient increase in bleeding** as oral vascular supply returns to normal and the masking effects of smoking are removed. Frame this as a sign of healing, not deterioration.

## 5. Modify periodontal management

- Mainstay: **good plaque control + regular high-quality supra- and subgingival debridement**, with adjunctive LA as needed
- Smokers with recession have higher root caries risk: **monitor diet and caries status; provide fluoride adjuncts**
- Periodontal management of smokers tends to **avoid surgery**, particularly hard or soft tissue **grafting**, due to reduced healing
- **Non-responding smokers**: consider referral

firstPrinciples.title: Subgingival flora re-establishes within three months even after thorough debridement
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Periodontitis is not curable in the way that caries is restored. The biological re-colonisation rate is what sets the maintenance interval.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why three-monthly recall exists

Evidence shows that even with good home care, a potentially pathogenic bacterial flora can re-establish itself at the base of a 5 mm + pocket **three months** after a thorough subgingival debridement, and this is one of the reasons for the three-monthly recall interval for periodontitis patients [1]. The recall interval is also driven by the need for continuous oral hygiene coaching and patient motivation, but the microbiology is the harder limit.

## Tailoring the interval

Intervals typically vary from 2 to 4 months initially, reviewed at each visit, and may be extended over time in patients with good compliance and stable supra- and subgingival environments [2]. The interval is set by what the disease and the patient demand, not by a fixed protocol.

This is one of the reasons for the three monthly recall interval for periodontitis patients.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Supportive periodontal therapy

firstPrinciples.title: Antibiotics are an adjunct to mechanical therapy, never a substitute
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Periodontitis is biofilm disease. Drugs cannot reach an organised biofilm; mechanical disruption has to come first.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The general rule

Systemic antibiotics should only ever be used as an adjunct to professionally administered mechanical therapy, and not in isolation [1]. There is no indication for systemic antibiotics when managing **chronic periodontitis** [2]. They may have a role in **aggressive periodontitis**, but the BSP suggests starting with non-surgical therapy alone and only adding antibiotics if the result is poor despite excellent oral hygiene and effective root surface debridement [3].

## What this means for prescribing decisions

Local delivery antibiotics are not first-line either: they are reserved for isolated pockets that have failed repeated conventional treatment, with no detectable calculus, in patients maintaining good plaque control, and the benefit is modest [4]. The default position in periodontics is mechanical therapy plus risk factor control; antibiotics are a narrow exception.

firstPrinciples.title: Behaviour change comes from within the patient, not from instruction
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Periodontal outcomes depend on daily home care, which is a habit, not a procedure. Habit change has to be patient-owned to last.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Motivation cannot be installed

Behavioural science research has demonstrated that lifestyle behaviour change occurs from within the patient, not externally from the practitioner. Motivation is not something that can be given or taught [1]. The clinician's role is to activate and encourage, using techniques that engage the patient to appreciate the information or skills needed to reach a goal.

## Why repeated lecturing backfires

A few selected, well-delivered words are more effective than a full lecture, and repeating instructions multiple times will not increase motivation: it may offend and decrease motivation [2]. Skills can be learned in minutes; habits take weeks or months [3]. Confidence in being able to clean is one of the strongest predictors of success, which is why the SDCEP TIPPS approach has the patient practise in the surgery and check confidence directly [4].

workflows.title: Detecting and managing peri-implant disease
workflows.overview:
Peri-implant disease is the umbrella term for two conditions: **peri-implant mucositis** (gingivitis equivalent, no bone loss) and **peri-implantitis** (periodontitis equivalent, progressive bone loss). The aetiology is bacterial plaque, but the implant tissues are less resistant to probing and the disease can progress more rapidly than around teeth.

## 1. Recognise that the BPE does not apply

Implant tissues are not connected to the surface like a periodontal ligament, so probing depths can be deeper in healthy sites. **Do not use the BPE for implants.** Instead:

- **Detailed probing (4 or 6 points)** around each implant
- Record bleeding and **suppuration**
- Probing depths recorded **at least annually**
- A periodontal probe will not damage the implant or soft tissues

## 2. Distinguish mucositis from peri-implantitis

### Peri-implant mucositis
- Inflammation of the peri-implant tissues
- Swelling, redness, tenderness, bleeding on probing
- **No concurrent bone loss**
- Affects ~**45%** of implant patients

### Peri-implantitis
- Progressive **loss of alveolar bone support** around the implant
- Affects ~**20%** of implant patients
- Can progress more rapidly than periodontitis

## 3. Apply prevention as the primary lever

- Recognise the aetiology is **bacterial**: meticulous peri-implant oral hygiene is essential
- Tools: **single-tufted brushes, interdental brushes, floss / superfloss**
- If the restoration is not amenable to plaque control, **disease risk is high**: design matters
- Control risk factors: smoking, diabetes, stress
- **Radiographs at implant placement and superstructure placement**; follow-ups guided by clinical findings

## 4. Treat mucositis to prevent progression

Mucositis is reversible. Improve OH around the implant, address risk factors, and remove plaque retention factors at the restoration.

## 5. Refer peri-implantitis

- **Peri-implantitis is difficult to treat**: refer to a specialist
- Treatment may be **non-surgical or surgical debridement** of the implant surfaces, **with or without adjunctive therapy**
- Counsel the patient that implants with peri-implant disease are **more likely to be lost**, even if disease is controlled, because recurrence is likely

## 6. Decide about implant placement in periodontal patients

Key rules:

- An implant is **a substitute for no tooth, not for a tooth**
- Patients unable or unwilling to maintain OH on natural teeth are **unlikely to manage implants better**
- Implants in periodontally susceptible patients carry **higher integration failure and long-term bone loss**
- **Even periodontally involved teeth can be more successful long-term than implants**
- Reasons to replace teeth in well-maintained patients: untreatable individual teeth (deep furcations, progressive infrabony defects, perio-endo lesions); posterior bite collapse or loss of anterior guidance; advanced or aggressive disease requiring clearance

firstPrinciples.title: Implants are biologically and clinically different from teeth, and the BPE does not apply
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Implant tissues are not connected to the implant surface like a periodontal ligament, so probing behaves differently and disease progresses faster.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why probing differs

Implants are susceptible to bacterial plaque just like teeth, but the tissues surrounding implants are not connected to the implant surface in the same way as those surrounding teeth and are less resistant to probing. This, combined with the implant's anatomical position relative to the bone and soft tissues, can produce **deeper probing depths in healthy sites** [1]. For this reason, the BPE is not appropriate for implants, and detailed probing (4 or 6 points) with bleeding and suppuration recorded around each implant is used instead [2].

## Why the disease moves faster

Peri-implantitis can be likened to periodontitis but is different in that it can progress more rapidly, which makes detection and management important [3]. Approximately 45% of implant patients have peri-implant mucositis and around 20% have peri-implantitis, so both are common, and design that prevents plaque control on the restoration directly raises disease risk [4].

This in combination with the anatomical position of the implant in relation to the bone and soft tissues may lead to deeper probing depths in healthy sites.

citations.quote: For this reason, the BPE is not appropriate for the assessment of implants. Detailed probing (four or six points) and the presence of any bleeding or suppuration should be measured around each implant.

firstPrinciples.title: An implant is a substitute for no tooth, not a substitute for a tooth
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The decision to extract a periodontally compromised tooth and place an implant is reframed once peri-implant disease prevalence is taken into account.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Periodontal susceptibility carries forward

If any non-modifiable risk factors, such as genetics, have played a part in the periodontal breakdown of an individual, those factors are likely to continue in the peri-implant tissue breakdown [1]. Patients unable or unwilling to maintain oral hygiene with natural teeth are unlikely to do better with implants [2].

## What the long-term data say

Implant integration failures and long-term bone loss are higher in patients with uncontrolled periodontal disease around remaining teeth, and peri-implant complications are significantly more common in periodontally susceptible but stabilised patients [3]. The conclusion the BSP draws is sharp: even periodontally involved teeth can be more successful in the long-term than dental implants [4].

## How to talk to the patient

An implant is not a substitute for a tooth, it is a substitute for no tooth [5]. Patients considering replacing a periodontally compromised tooth with an implant should be told the prognosis differential explicitly.

firstPrinciples.title: Periodontitis is associated with systemic disease, but causality is not established
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Periodontitis sits alongside cardiovascular disease and diabetes as common chronic non-communicable diseases. The link is real, but its direction and weight are still uncertain.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the link looks like

Gingival inflammation in periodontitis compromises the barrier function of the gingival epithelium, allowing bacteria, bacterial products and inflammatory products into the systemic circulation. In severe cases the wound area from periodontal inflammation can be as large as the palm of the hand, and this inflammation may be present for decades [1].

## Why causality is hard to nail down

Periodontitis and other common chronic non-communicable diseases share risk factors (smoking, obesity, diabetes, sedentary lifestyle, poor diet, increasing age). The impact of periodontitis on these disease processes is likely to be small, requiring large trials to demonstrate. There is also no consensus definition of periodontitis, which makes meta-analysis difficult [2].

## The clinically defensible message

Patients can be told periodontal disease is associated with other diseases, but it is not clear if it actually causes them. What is important for general health is also likely to be protective for periodontal health [3].

citations.quote: The biological mechanisms by which periodontitis might influence systemic health are linked to the fact that periodontitis causes gingival inflammation which compromises the barrier function of the gingival epithelium leading to an ingress of bacteria or bacterial products or inflammatory products into the systemic circulation. In severe cases, the wound area from periodontal inflammation can be as large as the palm of the hand.
citations.source: BSP Good Practitioners Guide (2016), Systemic disease and periodontal health

Secondly, the impact of periodontitis on these disease processes is likely to be small hence large-scale trials are needed to demonstrate this effect or lack of effect conclusively. Finally, there is a lack of consensus in the research community on a standard definition or criteria for periodontitis.
